PAST_PROGRESSIVE.text: Nana walked into the hallway during lunch and noticed that the door of an empty classroom was wide open. It was a cold day, and she thought the room would become too cold. She started to close the door, but a notice beside the handle caught her eye. It said, “Please keep this door open from 12:30 to 1:00.” Nana checked the lesson schedule too. The next class was a science activity that used a safe but strong-smelling liquid. The teacher wanted fresh air in the room before students arrived. Nana left the door open and moved a chair that was blocking part of the doorway. At one o'clock, the science teacher came and thanked her for following the notice. Nana had wanted to help by closing the door, but she learned that the open door was also part of a plan. Reading the notice before acting changed her decision.

MODAL_CAN.text: Yuma entered the classroom before afternoon lessons and saw one chair facing the window instead of the front board. He thought someone had moved it as a joke. The chair was in a walking space, so Yuma wanted to put it back at once. Then he noticed a note on the teacher's desk. It said that the art class would draw the old tree outside the west window. Yuma checked the afternoon plan on the board. Art was the first lesson, and the note asked students not to move the marked chair. A small piece of tape under the chair matched the mark on the note. Yuma left it where it was and moved his own bag away from the walking space. During art class, the teacher used that chair to show students a good viewing place. After the lesson, the chair went back to its desk. Yuma learned that something unusual in a room can have a clear purpose. He checked before changing it.

PAST_PROGRESSIVE.text: Kenta saw a yellow arrow on the floor near the stairs. It pointed away from the usual route to the classrooms. He first said, “This arrow is for a game.” Before following it, he read a sign on the wall. The sign said, “Health check today. Follow the yellow arrows to Room 5.” Kenta had a health check after lunch, so he followed the arrow. The route used a quieter hallway and kept students away from another class. He reached Room 5. A teacher was waiting there. The temporary arrow made sense after Kenta read the sign.

PASSIVE.text: The environmental committee placed two water-bottle return boxes in the school. After one week, the box near the gym was almost full, but the box beside the library had only a few bottles. Some students said the library box was unnecessary. Before removing it, the committee watched students in the area. They found that many students walked past the library box without noticing it because a tall plant covered the sign. The students moved the sign above the plant and added an arrow. During the next week, the number of returned bottles there doubled. The problem was not the location of the box but the way students saw it. They also asked five students to point to the box before and after the change. Four more students noticed it after the sign was moved.

MODAL_COULD.text: The tennis club sent practice reminders every morning at seven. Still, several members often forgot to bring special shoes for after-school practice. The club leader thought the messages were too short, but one student suggested checking when members actually read them. For five days, members recorded the time they opened the reminder. Most did not look at their phones before school. They read the message around lunch or after classes. At that time, they were at school and the shoes were at home. The club changed the reminder to eight o'clock the night before. During the following week, only one member forgot the shoes. The timing mattered more than adding more words. The club kept the message itself unchanged during the test, so they could compare the effect of timing fairly.

MODAL_COULD.text: Students at Midori Junior High wanted to reduce crowding between second and third period. There were two routes from the science rooms to the main classrooms. Route A was shorter by about thirty meters, so many students believed it was faster. A student team timed both routes for three days. When the halls were empty, Route A was faster. During class changes, however, students on Route A had to pass a narrow corner near the stairs. People from two directions met there and often stopped. Route B was longer but wider, and students could keep walking. The team also counted how many students reached the classroom within four minutes. Route B had the better result during busy times. Instead of telling everyone to avoid Route A, the school posted a suggestion: use Route B during class changes and Route A when the hall is quiet. The test showed that distance alone did not decide travel time. Teachers then repeated the timing test on a rainy day, when more students stayed inside. Route B still moved more steadily, which supported the recommendation.

MODAL_COULD.text: At the school festival cafe, customers chose drinks at a menu board beside the counter. A long line formed even when the workers were ready. The class first planned to add another worker. Then Emi watched customers for ten minutes. She saw that people could not read the menu until they reached the front because the line itself blocked the board. Many customers began choosing only after the worker asked for an order. The class moved a copy of the menu to the entrance of the line. Customers decided while they waited, and the line moved more smoothly. No extra worker was needed. The class solved the delay by changing where information appeared. They measured the line again at the next busy hour and found that customers reached the counter with an order already chosen.

MODAL_COULD.text: The cooking club used both a paper form and an online form for new members. The online form had more unanswered entries, so the club thought students disliked using phones. Riku compared the two forms carefully. The paper version asked for a name, class, and contact choice. The online version also asked, “What dish do you most want to make?” before students could finish. Some first-year students did not know what to write and stopped there. The club made that question optional and moved it to the end. After the change, almost everyone completed the online form. The problem was not the device; one required question was creating the difficulty. They kept both forms available, because some students still preferred paper even after the online form became easier.

After a light snowfall, students checked two walking routes from the station to school. Route A ran beside tall buildings, while Route B followed an open street. Route A was shorter, and teachers usually recommended it. By noon, most snow had melted, but several students reported slipping on Route A the next morning. The safety committee visited both routes at eight o'clock. Route B was wet but clear. On Route A, a shaded section still had thin ice because sunlight did not reach the ground early in the day. The committee returned at noon and found that the ice was gone. Instead of saying Route A was always dangerous, they changed the winter notice. It recommended Route B on cold mornings after snow and allowed either route later when conditions were clear. They also marked the shaded section on a map. Their decision used both place and time, not just the total distance. The committee asked students to report new icy spots for two weeks. No additional place caused repeated problems, so the map stayed focused on the shaded section.

PASSIVE.text: The school library created a shelf for short English books. The first shelf was used often, but the second shelf stayed almost full. The librarian thought the books on the second shelf were too difficult. A student team watched readers and asked a few questions. They learned that many students did not realize the second shelf was part of the same collection. Its category card was placed low behind a row of books. The team moved the card to eye level and added the same symbol used on the first shelf. During the next two weeks, more books from the second shelf were borrowed. The books had not changed; the way the shelf was labeled had.

MODAL_COULD.text: The broadcasting club made a lunchtime announcement about a school clean-up day. They added cheerful background music because they wanted students to listen. After the announcement, many students remembered the event but could not say where to meet. The club tested the recording with twelve students. When the music was loud, several missed the meeting place and start time. With softer music, almost all of them understood those details. The club kept the same words and the same short song but lowered the music during important information. The next announcement was easier to follow. The test showed that attractive sound should not hide the message it is meant to support. A short follow-up survey also showed that students still noticed the cheerful music, even at the lower volume.

MODAL_CAN.text: At the school festival shop, Class 2-1 used two checkout tables. Table A served each customer quickly, but its line often became long. Table B served people a little more slowly, yet its line disappeared sooner. The class first thought Table A needed another cashier. Mika watched the beginning of each sale period and found a different problem. Workers at Table A started setting out bags and change only after customers were already waiting. For the first five minutes, one cashier prepared supplies instead of serving people. Table B prepared everything ten minutes before opening. The class changed the setup order at Table A. Bags, coins, and price sheets were ready before the next sale period. The service speed for each customer did not change, but the early line became much shorter. The students learned that a fast process can still create a long wait if preparation begins too late. They improved the work before the first customer arrived. They repeated the change during the final sale period and saw the same pattern, so the improvement was not limited to one unusually quiet moment.

MODAL_COULD.text: Visitors to the school open day often asked where the gym was, even though a direction sign stood near the front gate. The student council first planned to make the letters larger. Before printing a new sign, they watched arriving families. From the gate, part of the sign was hidden by leaves from a small tree. People walking from the parking area could see it, but people from the station could not. The council moved the sign two meters to the left and tested it again from both directions. More visitors found the gym without asking. The original words were clear; the sign simply needed to be visible from the main approach. They left the tree in place and checked the sign again one week later to make sure new leaf growth had not hidden it.

GERUND.text: The basketball team often lost practice time because players stopped to look for balls, towels, or water after practice began. The captain suggested making practice fifteen minutes longer. Another student asked the team to test a smaller change first. For one week, everyone spent five quiet minutes before practice checking equipment and filling water bottles. The team recorded how often practice stopped later. The number of interruptions fell from an average of six to two. Players finished the planned drills without staying later. The team kept the five-minute check. They gained useful practice time by organizing the start, not by extending the end. The five minutes also gave injured players time to tell the captain what activities they needed to avoid that day.

HAVE_TO.text: A student group collected used books for a community reading room. Their first poster listed seven rules about accepted books. Even so, many donated books had to be returned. The students thought people had ignored the poster. They examined thirty rejected books and asked five donors what had confused them. Several donors had read the rules but did not understand phrases such as “good condition” and “recent reference material.” The group made a new poster with three main rules and pictures of examples. It showed a clean storybook as acceptable, a book with missing pages as unacceptable, and school reference books from the last five years as acceptable. They kept the detailed rules on a smaller sheet for volunteers. During the next collection, fewer books were rejected, and donors asked fewer questions. The students did not simply make the rules shorter. They separated information people needed before donating from details volunteers needed while checking books. Volunteers recorded the reasons for every rejected book during the second collection. Water damage, not unclear categories, became the most common reason after the redesign.

ADJECTIVE_TO_INFINITIVE.text: A community study room opened on Saturdays, but first-time visitors often walked past its entrance. The door looked like a staff door and stayed closed to keep the room quiet. Students helping there watched the hallway and spoke with visitors. They found that a small “Study Room” label was easy to miss, especially from the stairs. The students added a welcome sign at eye level and placed a small open sign beside the handle when the room was available. They did not leave the door open because noise would enter. The next Saturday, more visitors entered without asking for help. Clear signs made the entrance feel public while the room stayed quiet. They also placed the opening hours below the welcome sign, which prevented people from trying the door after the room had closed.

MODAL_COULD.text: There were four students with the same two-hour study plan before a test. They began with easy review, then did difficult math, and finished with vocabulary. After three days, they compared concentration notes. All four felt most tired during math, which began after seventy minutes. They first considered adding another study hour. Instead, they moved math to the first forty minutes and put easy review later. The total study time stayed two hours. During the next three days, the students completed more math problems and made fewer careless mistakes. They learned that changing the order of tasks could help more than simply making the plan longer. The students kept the same breaks and subjects, allowing them to judge the effect of task order instead of several changes at once.

WANT_TO.text: The school festival wanted to reduce trash from food stalls. One class suggested using reusable plates everywhere, while another worried about washing time. The planning team ran a small trial at three stalls. At the curry stall, most customers ate near the return station, and 92 percent of plates came back quickly. At the snack stall near the field, many customers walked away while eating, and only 61 percent returned plates to the correct place. The dessert stall had a good return rate but created a long washing line during one busy hour. The team decided not to use one system for every stall. They chose reusable plates for curry, improved the washing schedule for dessert, and kept paper containers at the field snack stall while adding a recycling box. The plan reduced waste without creating a plate shortage. The trial showed that a useful environmental idea still needed to fit how each stall actually worked. The team posted simple return instructions at the two reusable-plate stalls and counted missing plates at closing time. Only a few were unreturned, so the next event kept the mixed system.

MODAL_COULD.text: The student council made an online survey about the school cafeteria. Many students opened it, but fewer than half reached the main food questions. The council first thought students were not interested in lunch. Then they checked where people stopped. The first page asked for grade, club, usual lunch place, and several optional comments before the cafeteria questions began. Younger students often left during that page. The council kept only grade and usual lunch place at the start and moved the other questions to the end. In the next survey, far more students reached the food section. The council improved completion by shortening the path to the questions that mattered most. They also displayed a progress bar, so students could see that the remaining questions were short after the main section.

A community pantry stored milk and prepared food in two refrigerators. Volunteers noticed that food from Refrigerator B was sometimes thrown away before its use-by date because the temperature record showed short rises above the target range. Some people wanted to replace the refrigerator immediately. A group of students examined one month of temperature logs together with delivery times. Most rises happened between 4:00 and 4:30 p.m., when several boxes were delivered and the door stayed open while volunteers sorted food. On days without a large delivery, the temperature remained stable. The students tested a new process: boxes were sorted on a table first, and the refrigerator door was opened only when items were ready to be placed inside. The next week's log showed smaller and shorter temperature rises. A technician still checked the refrigerator and found no mechanical problem. The pantry kept the refrigerator but changed its delivery routine. By comparing time records with actual work, the students avoided replacing equipment that was working correctly and helped reduce food loss. The students also compared how long the door remained open on ordinary days. It was usually less than two minutes, but large-delivery days averaged nearly nine minutes. They placed a rolling cart beside the sorting table so chilled items could be grouped together before the door opened. MODAL_CAN.text: Students preparing a bilingual safety guide compared the Japanese and English notices for a school workshop. One English sentence said that “all visitors” must wear protective glasses near the cutting machine. The Japanese original, however, required glasses only for visitors who entered the marked work area. The word “all” had been added during an earlier rewrite. It made the English rule stricter than the original and could confuse people waiting outside the work area. The students checked the teacher's official rule and changed the English notice to match it. They also asked another student to read both versions independently. The final pair gave the same condition in both languages. The group learned that adding a familiar word can still change the meaning of a safety message. To prevent the same problem later, the team marked conditions such as “in the work area” in a separate review column. Translators had to check that column before approving a sentence. The teacher preferred this method because it protected the exact rule without forcing both languages to use identical word order.

MODAL_COULD.text: A town planned a Saturday walking event from Harbor Station to the old lighthouse. The usual seaside path was easy to follow, but part of it would be closed from 10:30 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. for repair work. Organizers had to choose a route for three groups leaving the station at 9:40, 10:20, and 11:00. A tide table also showed that the lower beach path could not be used safely after 10:45 because the tide would cover a narrow section. A shuttle bus left the market square for the lighthouse at 10:50 and 11:50. The first group could use the seaside path and reach the lighthouse before the closure. The second group would reach the repair area after the closure, and the beach path would become unsafe before the group finished it. Organizers therefore directed that group to the market square and the 10:50 shuttle. The third group used the inland road to the market square and took the 11:50 shuttle. The route board explained why different groups received different directions. The safest plan did not depend on distance alone; departure time, construction, tide, and bus service all had to be considered together. The organizers tested the plan by estimating walking times. The seaside route normally took forty minutes, the inland walk to the market square took twenty-five minutes, and the lower beach path needed about thirty-five minutes. This confirmed that the 10:20 group could not simply hurry through the closed section. They also considered asking that group to wait until 1:00, but that would delay lunch and separate them from the event program. The shuttle solution kept their arrival close to the other groups. On the route board, a blue line showed the normal seaside route, a green line showed the inland route, and a red mark identified the closed section. Next to the tide table, organizers added a note explaining that “open now” did not mean “safe for the whole walk.” Volunteers at Harbor Station received the same information so they could answer questions consistently. On the event morning, each group leader checked the current board before departure because weather or repair work could still change the plan.

SUPERLATIVE.text: A school newspaper interviewed a local baker about reducing plastic bags. In a draft article, the baker was quoted as saying, “Customers do not want paper bags.” The statement sounded clear, but one student remembered a longer answer. The team listened to the original recording. The baker had actually said, “Some customers do not want paper bags on rainy days because they worry about water, but most accept them when we explain the new covers.” The first draft had kept only the beginning and changed the impression of the interview. The students replaced the short quote with a summary that included both the concern and the condition under which customers accepted paper bags. They also saved the recording time beside their notes. The correction made the article less dramatic but more accurate. The editor then asked each writer to label notes as direct quote, summary, or background fact. That small change made it easier to see when shortened wording needed to be checked against the recording before publication.

MODAL_SHOULD.text: Two student groups surveyed use of Sakura Park and reached different conclusions. Group A visited on a sunny Saturday afternoon and counted many families near the playground. Group B visited on a cloudy Tuesday morning and found mostly older adults walking near the pond. At first, each group believed the other had counted incorrectly. They compared their survey sheets and discovered that both groups had followed the same counting method. The difference came from when and where they had observed the park. To obtain a broader picture, the students returned four times: weekday morning, weekday afternoon, weekend morning, and weekend afternoon. They counted users in the playground, pond path, and open field separately. The combined results showed that the park served different groups at different times. Families were common near the playground on weekends, while walkers used the pond path more steadily through the week. Instead of choosing one survey as correct, the students explained the conditions behind both. Their final report recommended collecting data across several time periods before changing park facilities. The students also compared weather within the new survey. Weekend afternoon use dropped during light rain, while the pond path still had several regular walkers. This helped them avoid treating every difference as a weekday-versus-weekend effect. They included the weather beside each count in the final table and wrote that future surveys should use the same categories. A park manager said the richer record was more useful. It showed how many people came and which spaces they used under different conditions.

MODAL_COULD.text: A class of fifty-four students planned a visit to a science center. They would arrive at 10:00 and leave at 12:30. The center offered a robotics workshop at 10:20 and 11:20. The workshop room held eighteen students. A planetarium show began at 10:30 and 11:30, and its room held thirty-six. The class was divided into three groups of eighteen. Group A could attend robotics at 10:20 while Groups B and C watched the 10:30 planetarium show together. At 11:20, Group B could attend robotics. Group A would use the exhibition floor, and Group C would remain there until the 11:30 planetarium show was no longer useful for the whole group because only thirty minutes would remain before departure. The students changed the plan: Group C attended robotics at 11:20 instead of Group B, while Group B used the exhibition floor. Group C had already seen the 10:30 planetarium show with Group B, so this created a conflict. They checked the schedule again and realized only two robotics sessions were available, so not all three groups could take robotics. The final plan gave robotics to Groups A and B and the planetarium to all students in two rotations, while Group C used an interactive lab instead of robotics. The class chose a plan that respected capacities and accepted that every group could not do every activity. The class then built a timetable for every twenty-minute block. From 10:00 to 10:20, all groups received orientation. Group A entered robotics at 10:20, while Groups B and C went to the 10:30 planetarium. After that show, Group B reached the 11:20 robotics workshop in time. Group C moved to the interactive lab, where eighteen students fit comfortably. Group A used the exhibition floor after robotics. At 11:30, Group A joined other visitors in the planetarium because enough seats remained, while Groups B and C continued activities they had not yet completed. The teacher checked walking time between rooms and required a ten-minute movement margin, so no group was scheduled in two distant places back-to-back. The final chart used three colors, one for each group, and showed meeting points as well as activity times. Students accepted that Group C would not do robotics because trying to force all three groups into two workshops would violate the room capacity. Instead, the interactive lab gave that group a hands-on activity of similar length. Everyone returned to the entrance by 12:20, leaving ten minutes for attendance before departure.

BECAUSE_CLAUSE.text: Students studied three bicycle racks near a community center. Rack A was used by twenty-five people a day and had light rust on two bars. Rack B was used by only eight people, but users said it was convenient because it stood beside the main entrance. Rack C was almost new, yet it was used by just three people because rainwater collected around it after storms. A maintenance company estimated that repairing Rack A would cost much less than replacing it. Moving Rack C to higher ground would cost more than a small repair but less than buying a new rack. The students recommended repairing Rack A, keeping Rack B as it was, and moving Rack C. They did not rank the racks only by age or appearance. Use, location, cost, and the cause of each problem led to different choices. Six months later, Rack C was used more often in its drier location, while Rack A remained safe after repair. The mixed plan used the budget where it solved an actual problem. The students also counted empty spaces at different times instead of relying on one daily average. Rack B filled briefly during evening meetings, which explained why users valued its position despite the lower average. For Rack C, they observed where riders parked when puddles formed and found several bicycles attached to a fence on higher ground. After moving Rack C, those bicycles shifted to the rack. The follow-up supported the idea that poor use had reflected the wet location rather than a lack of demand.

MODAL_COULD.text: A community market planned outdoor activities from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The weather forecast showed light rain before 10:00, a dry period from 10:00 to noon, and heavier rain after 12:30. The site map had two covered areas: a small tent for thirty people and a large hall for eighty. A children's craft activity needed forty seats and was scheduled for 9:30. A music performance expected seventy visitors at 11:00, and a local food talk for twenty-five people was planned at 1:00. Organizers could not simply move every event indoors because the hall was being used for market tables until 10:30. They moved the craft activity to 10:15 in the hall after some tables were cleared. The 11:00 music performance stayed outdoors during the dry period, with the hall ready as a backup. The 1:00 food talk moved to the small tent because its expected audience fit the space and heavier rain was likely. The final notice explained the changes and asked visitors to check the board at 10:45 for the music decision. By matching weather, capacity, and room availability, the organizers created a schedule that could change safely without cancelling the whole market. The team also prepared decision rules instead of relying on a last-minute guess. If rain at 10:45 was only light and radar showed the dry period continuing, the music performance would stay outside. If heavier rain arrived early, staff would move chairs into the hall and delay the start by ten minutes. A volunteer counted available hall seats after the market tables were reduced, confirming that seventy visitors could enter without blocking exits. For the craft activity, families registered at the information desk so organizers knew whether the forty-seat estimate remained reasonable. The small tent was reserved for the food talk from 12:40, leaving twenty minutes for setup before the speaker began. Signs at the entrance used the same activity names and times as the printed program, reducing confusion when a location changed. After the market, organizers compared attendance with the revised schedule and found that no activity had to be cancelled. They saved the weather-and-capacity table as a model for future outdoor events, while noting that new forecasts must always replace the old numbers.

MODAL_COULD.text: A poster in the school hall said, “Seventy percent of students prefer digital books.” The number was repeated in a club presentation, but Aya wanted to see the original survey. She found that the actual question had been, “When carrying three or more textbooks, would you prefer a digital version for at least one book?” Seventy percent had answered yes. The survey did not ask whether students preferred digital books in general. The club changed its presentation to say that many students wanted a digital option when carrying several textbooks. The percentage remained the same, but the claim became narrower and matched the question that produced the number. Aya learned that a number cannot be understood fully without knowing what was asked. The club added the original survey question below the graph so readers could judge the number themselves. They also stopped using the word “prefer” by itself when a choice depended on a particular situation.

MODAL_COULD.text: A community garden had two vegetable beds that produced very different amounts of tomatoes. Bed A produced almost twice as many as Bed B, and some volunteers wanted to replace the soil in Bed B. Students examined the garden records before agreeing. The soil tests from both beds were similar, but the sunlight records were not. A new building cast shade over Bed B for part of the afternoon, while Bed A received direct sun for several more hours. The students also checked growth notes from leafy vegetables. Those plants had grown well in Bed B even after the building was completed. The group proposed planting more tomatoes in Bed A and using Bed B for vegetables that could grow with less direct sun. They also planned one small tomato test in Bed B rather than removing tomatoes completely. The next season, total harvest from the two beds increased. The students did not treat lower tomato production as proof of poor soil. By comparing several records, they found that the two beds had different strengths and adjusted planting to match them. To test the new plan fairly, volunteers recorded planting dates, watering, and harvest weights for both beds. They used the same tomato variety in the small Bed B test, so a different variety would not confuse the comparison. The test tomatoes in Bed B produced less fruit but remained healthy, while leafy vegetables used the shaded space effectively. These results supported keeping a small experiment while using most of each bed for crops suited to its light conditions.

MODAL_COULD.text: A bag disappeared from a bench during a school event. Three students gave different accounts. Student A said she saw the bag on the bench at 1:10. Student B said a tall person carried a dark bag away at about 1:20. Student C said the owner returned at 1:25 and looked surprised. Some committee members immediately decided that the tall person had taken the missing bag. Others pointed out that Student B had not seen the bench and could not identify the bag. The committee separated direct observations from guesses. They checked a photo taken at 1:18 and saw the missing bag still on the bench. Later, the owner found it at the information desk, where a staff member had moved it for safety. The careful timeline prevented an unsupported accusation. The committee wrote the confirmed times in one column and uncertain descriptions in another. This made it clear that height and bag color were useful leads but not proof of identity. Staff members later adopted the same format for other lost-property reports.

COMPARATIVE.text: Museum volunteers tested two versions of an audio tour. Version A gave the information quickly with almost no pause. Version B used the same information but included long pauses after every sentence. Visitors using Version A often finished, but some said they needed more time to look at objects. Visitors using Version B had enough looking time but sometimes felt the tour was slow and stopped it. The team created Version C with short pauses only after important descriptions and before visitors moved to the next object. In a new test, more visitors completed the tour and reported that the pace felt comfortable. The team did not remove historical information; it changed when listeners were given time to look. The volunteers also checked whether age affected the result. Younger and older visitors preferred slightly different speeds, but both groups completed Version C more often than Version B. The museum therefore kept one main version and added a pause button reminder at the start for anyone who wanted extra viewing time.

MODAL_COULD.text: After a large storm warning, a community center prepared three rooms as a temporary shelter. Room A held forty people and was closest to the entrance. Room B held twenty and had a sink. Room C held thirty and was the quietest room. Four family groups were expected: twelve older adults, eight families with small children totaling twenty-four people, ten adults who needed no special support, and six people who used mobility aids. Supplies would arrive in two deliveries. Water and blankets would arrive at 5:00 p.m., while baby supplies and extra floor mats would arrive at 6:30. The planning students placed the six people using mobility aids and twelve older adults in Room A because it had the easiest entrance route. The twenty-four people in families with small children could not fit in Room B, even though its sink was useful. They used Room C for most of those families and placed four people from that group in Room B with the ten other adults. The students reserved space near Room B's sink for baby-care use after the 6:30 delivery. Their plan also kept each room below capacity and left a clear path to the entrance. The room choices balanced access, quiet, useful facilities, family size, and delivery timing rather than giving every special group the room with the most obvious feature. The students then tested the room plan against two changes. First, they assumed four additional adults might arrive after 6:00. Rooms A and B still had enough unused capacity for them without moving the families. Second, they considered what would happen if the 6:30 delivery was delayed. Baby-care space near the sink would still be available, but volunteers would need to keep a small emergency set from existing supplies. The entrance map marked a wide route to Room A and prohibited boxes from being stored along it. Room C received a quiet-area sign because young children might sleep there, while louder information announcements were made near Rooms A and B. Each room leader received a list showing current room totals, free spaces, and the location of water after the first delivery. The final plan was not permanent; students wrote that assignments should change if a person's health or mobility needs changed. By checking both capacity and possible disruptions, they made the shelter plan flexible rather than merely fitting everyone into the rooms once.

MODAL_COULD.text: The newspaper club prepared a headline saying, “New Study Space Improves Learning for Everyone.” The headline was based on a graph showing that students who used the room reported higher concentration than before. Before publishing, one member checked the survey details. Only forty students had answered, and all of them were regular users of the new room. The survey did not include students who studied elsewhere, and it measured reported concentration rather than test scores. The club changed the headline to “Regular Users Report Better Concentration in New Study Space.” The graph stayed in the article, but the text explained who had answered and what had been measured. The revised headline was less dramatic, yet it matched the evidence instead of claiming a result for every student. The article also linked the graph title directly to the survey question and stated the number of respondents. Readers could then see the difference between a report about regular users and a claim about the whole school.

MODAL_COULD.text: Students compared water-quality records from a local stream in spring and autumn. The autumn sheet showed clearer water and a lower reading for one pollution indicator. Some students wanted to report that the stream had improved. Before writing the conclusion, the group checked the measurement conditions. The spring sample had been taken the morning after heavy rain, while the autumn sample came after five dry days. The sampling times were also different. Rain could carry soil and other material into the stream, so the two measurements were not directly comparable. The students collected another sample after similar dry weather and at the same time of day as the autumn test. The new result was closer to the autumn record. Their report said the first comparison was inconclusive and explained what conditions needed to match before judging long-term change. The group scheduled future sampling for the first Friday of each month at the same hour and planned to record recent rainfall beside every result. They noted that matching conditions would not remove every difference, but it would make changes easier to interpret.
